title: Migrations
summary: How a database evolves with your model: migration files, the history table, and the dotnet ef commands.

steps.title: What a migration is
body: Your model changes over time: a new property, a renamed table, a new index. A database full of real data cannot be dropped and recreated each time. **Migrations** record each change as a small class with two methods:
```csharp
public partial class AddPhone : Migration
protected override void Up(MigrationBuilder migration)
=> migration.AddColumn<string>(name: "Phone", table: "Customers", nullable: true);
protected override void Down(MigrationBuilder migration)
=> migration.DropColumn(name: "Phone", table: "Customers");

`Up` moves the database forward; `Down` undoes it. Next to the migrations sits a **model snapshot**: what the model looked like after the last migration. When you add a migration, EF Core compares your current model with that snapshot and writes the difference for you.
The database keeps a table, **`__EFMigrationsHistory`**, listing the migrations already applied. Applying migrations means: run `Up` for every migration not in that table, in order, and record each.

steps.title: The commands
body: Migrations are made with the **EF Core tools**, a `dotnet` command-line tool (install once with `dotnet tool install --global dotnet-ef`) plus the `Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Design` package in your project.
| Command | Does |
| `dotnet ef migrations add AddPhone` | compare model and snapshot, write `AddPhone.cs` and update the snapshot |
| `dotnet ef database update` | apply every pending migration to the database |
| `dotnet ef database update Initial` | migrate forwards **or back** to that migration (running `Down`s) |
| `dotnet ef migrations list` | show migrations, and which are applied |
| `dotnet ef migrations remove` | delete the last migration, if it is not applied yet |
| `dotnet ef migrations script --idempotent` | write the SQL for all migrations, safe to run on any version |
These are run in a terminal in your project folder, not from code. (The code steps here cannot run them, so this lesson shows what they produce instead.)
> **Tip:** Always **read** a generated migration before applying it. A renamed property can come out as "drop column, add column", which loses the data; fix it to `RenameColumn` by hand.

steps.explain: `add` and `remove` change files in your project; `database update` changes a database; `script` changes nothing and prints SQL.

steps.prompt: How does `dotnet ef database update` know which migrations a database still needs?
options: It reads the `__EFMigrationsHistory` table in that database
It compares the tables in the database with the model
It runs every migration again, and each skips itself if not needed
steps.explain: The history table lists applied migrations by id. Everything in your project that is not in that list is pending. The snapshot is only used when *adding* a migration.

steps.title: Applying migrations from code
body: `db.Database.Migrate()` does what `dotnet ef database update` does, from inside your program: it applies every pending migration. The migrations are just classes in your assembly, found by two attributes:
```csharp
[DbContext(typeof(ShopDb))]                 // which context it belongs to
[Migration("20260201000000_AddPhone")]      // its id: a timestamp, then the name
class AddPhone : Migration { ... }
The ids sort by time, which is the order they run in.

Calling `Migrate()` at app start is convenient for small apps and tests. For real production databases, teams usually apply a reviewed **SQL script** (`migrations script --idempotent`) or a **migration bundle** (`dotnet ef migrations bundle`) as a deployment step, so that several app instances never race to migrate the same database at start-up.
> **Tip:** `Migrate()` and `EnsureCreated()` do not mix: a database made by `EnsureCreated` has no history table.

steps.explain: A brand-new database has both migrations pending. `Migrate` runs `Initial`, then `AddPhone`, and records both in `__EFMigrationsHistory`. The new column is there to store the phone number.

steps.title: Write a migration
prompt: The tests give you the `ShopDb` context and its `Initial` migration from the last card. The `Customer` class has since grown an `Email` (`string`, required) and a `Loyalty` (`int`, required) property, and needs an index.
Write the next migration, `AddEmailAndLoyalty`, with id `"20260301000000_AddEmailAndLoyalty"`:

- `Up`: add `Email` (`string`, not nullable, `defaultValue: ""`) and `Loyalty` (`int`, not nullable, `defaultValue: 0`) to `Customers`, and create a **unique** index named `IX_Customers_Email` on `Email` (`migration.CreateIndex(name: ..., table: ..., column: ..., unique: true)`).

- `Down`: drop the index (`DropIndex`), then both columns. SQLite can only alter tables in limited ways, so `migration.DropColumn` needs information from the model snapshot that a hand-written migration does not have: drop each column with raw SQL instead, `migration.Sql("ALTER TABLE Customers DROP COLUMN Loyalty");`.
The tests migrate a database that already holds a customer, migrate back down to `Initial` and up again.
solution: migration.Sql("ALTER TABLE Customers DROP COLUMN Loyalty");
migration.Sql("ALTER TABLE Customers DROP COLUMN Email");
template: Dojo.Eq("the existing customer got the default email", "", dojoDb.Customers.Where(c => c.Name == "Old customer").Select(c => c.Email).Single());
Dojo.Throws<DbUpdateException>("the email index is unique", () => dojoDb.SaveChanges());
dojoDb.Database.ExecuteSql($"DELETE FROM Customers WHERE Name = 'Ana'");   // two blank emails would break the unique index on the way back up
Dojo.Eq("Down rolls back to Initial", "20260101000000_Initial", string.Join(",", dojoDb.Database.GetAppliedMigrations()));
Dojo.Eq("the customers survive the round trip", 1, dojoDb.Database.SqlQuery<int>($"SELECT COUNT(*) AS Value FROM Customers").ToList().Single());
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options
protected override void Down(MigrationBuilder migration) => migration.DropTable("Customers");
hints: `Down` undoes `Up` in reverse order: index first, then the columns.
